title: The History of Glam Rock and How It Put an End to the Hippie Era
description:
in History, Music |   	August 7th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

Cast your mind back to the dis­tant year 2021 and recall, if you will, its music,
body:
in History, Music |   	August 7th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

Cast your mind back to the dis­tant year 2021 and recall, if you will, its music, its fash­ions, the obses­sions of its youth. This prob­a­bly won’t be a dif­fi­cult task, since in most respects — the damp­en­ing effects of the pan­dem­ic notwith­stand­ing — none of those aspects of pop­u­lar cul­ture seem any dif­fer­ent today. Yet rough­ly the same time span sep­a­rat­ed Scott McKen­zie’s “San Fran­cis­co (Be Sure to Wear Flow­ers in Your Hair)” and David Bowie’s “Star­man.” 1967 was the year of the Sum­mer of Love; by 1972, accord­ing to most reck­on­ings, the cul­tur­al era known as the Six­ties was, if not quite over, then at least clear­ly in its final days. The hip­pies were on their way down, and glam rock­ers had arisen to take their place with a vengeance.
In less than half an hour, the new video from Band­splain­ing tells the whole sto­ry of glam rock, “the gen­der-bend­ing pro­to-punk move­ment that was hat­ed by the press and crim­i­nal­ly under­played in the U.S.” It begins in the 1970s, a time when the mar­ket for long-play­ing records was robust, but sin­gles had fall­en behind as a youth-ori­ent­ed pop-cul­tur­al form.
Into that vac­u­um stepped T. Rex, a one­time avant-garde folk duo rein­vent­ed as a straight-ahead rock band bent on reviv­ing that genre as it row­di­ly was before the Bea­t­les came along. When they hit it big, oth­er acts imi­tat­ed not just their bluesy sound, but the androg­y­nous, brazen­ly fab­ri­ca­tion-for­ward image of front­man Marc Bolan. Prac­ti­cal­ly overnight, the name of the game changed from earnest self-expres­sion to out­landish self-cre­ation.
Oth­er bands reshaped by this glam rock move­ment, as it was soon dubbed in the British media, includ­ed Slade, The Sweet, and Mott the Hoople. “My broth­er’s back at home with his Bea­t­les and his Stones,” sang that last out­fit in their break­out hit. “We nev­er got it off on that rev­o­lu­tion stuff.” That song, “All the Young Dudes,” had been writ­ten by the sin­gle most defin­ing glam-rock fig­ure: David Bowie, who him­self shot to promi­nence in the thor­ough­ly anti-Six­ties guise of Zig­gy Star­dust, the bisex­u­al, syn­thet­ics-clad rock­er from out­er space who swag­gered as if already famous across the uni­verse. With­in a few years, Bowie’s anten­na for the zeit­geist would have him retir­ing Zig­gy Star­dust and ditch­ing glam rock, a genre whose flame burned as bril­liant­ly — and indeed gar­ish­ly — as it did briefly. But in pop music, its char­ac­ter­is­tic lack of sociopo­lit­i­cal ideals, obses­sion with fame, and casu­al rela­tion­ship with real­i­ty were here to stay.

Based in Seoul, Col­in Marshall writes and broad­casts on cities, lan­guage, and cul­ture. He’s the author of the newslet­ter Books on Cities as well as the books 한국 요약 금지 (No Sum­ma­riz­ing Korea) and Kore­an Newtro. Fol­low him on the social net­work for­mer­ly known as Twit­ter at @colinmarshall.

title: Under Glass Cloches, Amber Cowan Nests Enchanting Flameworked Scenes
description: Known for her lush assemblages of flameworked glass, Amber Cowan reimagines a ubiquitous yet fragile medium. Flowers, filigree, and colorful baubl
body:
Known for her lush assemblages of flameworked glass, Amber Cowan reimagines a ubiquitous yet fragile medium. Flowers, filigree, and colorful baubles cluster into dense compositions that invoke fairytale narratives and whimsical nature scenes. Cowan typically works with industrial scraps, antiques, and other offcasts, which allows her to draw on products and colorways that are no longer in production.
Currently leaning into cloche and coupe sculptures alongside her wall-based works, the Philadelphia-based artist is preparing for several upcoming exhibitions, including at San Francisco’s Museum of Craft and Design in September and Design Miami in December. Her work is on view now in The Passion of Collecting at The Baker Museum in Naples, Florida, and you can find more on Instagram.

title: A Menagerie of Animal Sculptures by 50+ Artists Populate 'The Ark'
description: The term “ark” invariably conjures images of the monumental boat onto which pairs of animals were stewarded prior to a cataclysmic, biblical flood
body:
The term “ark” invariably conjures images of the monumental boat onto which pairs of animals were stewarded prior to a cataclysmic, biblical flood. It’s a reference that feels apt amid the climate crisis and our planet’s rising sea levels, although in this case, the melting ice caps and creeping tides are down to us. The large-scale exhibition titled The Ark at Powerhouse Arts asks, will we care for the future of our planet the way we care for the animals we love?
The presentation draws directly on the myth if The Deluge from Genesis, “an event of epic scale that becomes a metaphor for the present moment, where environmental and social upheaval converge,” says a statement. “Throughout the exhibition—experienced in the round, in close proximity, and at monumental scale—the animals function as both protagonists and interlocutors.”
Installation view of ‘The Ark’ at Powerhouse Arts, Summer 2026. Photo by Xavier Petromelis
Colossal readers may recognize the work of Kiki Smith, Nichola Theakston, Anthony Theakston, Wangechi Mutu, Jeffrey Gibson, and more. In all, more than 50 artists are represented through 90 sculptures and installations. The pieces run the gamut of materials, from wood and stone carvings to cast bronze and resin. A group of pigeons by Maurizio Cattelan perch on structural beams and both Nichola and Anthony Theakstons’ bronzes speak to the sacredness of animals, while John O’Reilly’s rendition of an emaciated female dog crouching over her pup plucks a heart-rending chord. Throughout the exhibition, emotional evocations span joy, amazement, humor, trepidation, and grief.
Curated by artist Eric Fischl, the show was first staged at The Church in Sag Harbor, a historical whaling town. Now in Brooklyn, the The Ark lands in the former warehouse space of Powerhouse Arts, a nonprofit dedicated to fabrication and production, on the Gowanus Canal. The building is known as the “Batcave” and sits adjacent to what’s designated by the Environmental Protection Agency as a Superfund site, a heavily polluted area in need of concerted cleanup efforts.
The physical location and its surroundings present a post-industrial background to a show about nature, the environment, and material exploration. Visitors are invited to walk through a room filled with animals from floor to ceiling, invoking elements of surprise and wonder. Powerhouse Arts adds, “Rather than framing environmental themes through notions of crisis and urgency alone, the exhibition centers on relationships and intimate encounters.”
The Ark continues through August 30 in Brooklyn. Find more on the organization’s Instagram.
John O’Reilly, “Intertwined” (2012), white: resin graphite; black: resin porcelain and bone powder, 24 x 21 1/2 x 31 1/2 inches (white dog), 5 x 21 1/4 x 16 1/4 inches (black dog). Photo by Gary Mamay, courtesy of Eric Fischl and April Gornik
Deborah Butterfield. Installation view of ‘The Ark’ at Powerhouse Arts, Summer 2026. Photo by Xavier Petromelis
William Kent, “Bittem and Beetle” (1968), black Italian slate, 10 5/8 x 17 1/2 x 1/4 inches. Photo by Cloe Poisson, courtesy of the William Kent Art Foundation
Jeffrey Gibson. Installation view of ‘The Ark’ at Powerhouse Arts, Summer 2026. Photo by Xavier Petromelis

title: 2,300-Year-Old Fragment of Homer’s “Odyssey” Now on View at The Met
description:
News
                The papyrus fragment contains three lines from Book 20 of the epic that don’t appear in the modern text.
body:
News
                The papyrus fragment contains three lines from Book 20 of the epic that don’t appear in the modern text.
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
            A papyrus fragment of Homer's Odyssey on view at The Metropolitan Museum of Art (photo Rebecca Schear, all courtesy The Met)
    
        
            The subway trek to the Upper East Side is slightly easier than Odysseus's journey across the Mediterranean, provided the 6 train is running. For those who prevail, their reward will be plentiful: A 2,300-year-old papyrus fragment containing parts of Homer's Odyssey is now on view at the Metropolitan Museum of Art. The institution announced this week that the object would emerge from its long retirement on August 5. The fragment is now on public view at the museum in Gallery 162.In a video accompanying The Met's announcement, Séan Hemingway, curator in charge of Greek and Roman art, described the papyrus as “the earliest preserved fragment of Homer's Odyssey that we have today.”

title: A View From the Easel
description:
Community
                “Going back there is a psychological, conscious choice to enter the space and interact with the energy.”
body:
Community
                “Going back there is a psychological, conscious choice to enter the space and interact with the energy.”
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
        
            Welcome to the 349th installment of A View From the Easel, a series in which artists reflect on their workspace. This week, Lilit Martirosyan summons the memories embedded in wool and soil while the sounds of opera arias fill her studio.Want to take part? Check out our submission guidelines and share a bit about your studio with us through this form! All mediums and workspaces are welcome, including your home studio.Lilit Martirosyan, Yerevan, ArmeniaHow long have you been working in this space?Around three and a half years.Describe an average day in your studio.It’s 8 am and the dazzling waves of the sun are penetrating through the floor-to-ceiling window frame, leaving a checkered shadow on the floor. It’s relatively quiet and the studio stays filled with sunlight till 1pm, so I try to spend some good morning hours there and catch the light. Sometimes when I work on a project I get completely consumed, staying in till late evening, and other times when I’m in between works it’s more about sketching, slow idea and material exploration, and browsing of the artist books I have around. I work in different media: installation, painting, printmaking … So my routine and materials change a lot, from physical work of sifting the soil to aesthetic surface experimentation with oil paint. When working on a series I often juggle between artworks while they dry but generally prefer finishing a project before jumping to something else. There is always something playing in the background. I’m very much into old music, classic rock, ’30s jazz, and recently opera arias that help me to phase away.How does the space affect your work?I am much more focused in the studio than anywhere else. I like that my living space is separate from my artistic space and I can be as messy as I want and free in my process, letting people in only at the stage of the work I’m comfortable for them to see. While the ideas and inspiration can come from anywhere, it is always best for me to do the making in the studio without any distraction and around my own creative “artifacts.” It is like a saving bank of creative energy that you accumulate during your work, so going back there is a psychological, conscious choice to enter the space and interact with the energy.How do you interact with the environment outside your studio?The studio is in the industrial part of the city, always buzzing with noise, though it has its charm once you get used to it. It is situated in a former silk factory building from the Soviet era. Now, the first floor is a gold market and the rest is occupied by all kinds of small factories and studios. There are some artist studios but they are scattered around the building and everyone comes and goes at their own pace.What do you love about your studio?I love that it has high ceilings, it is practically a perfect cube, and the big window. For me it is a welcoming and not abusive space in the sense that I can always start fresh without the aggravation of the past work.What do you wish were different?I wish it were closer to my place. I usually commute around 40 minutes but I try to treat it like a legal time out, a routine when you can catch up on something you have been putting off or just rest and people-watch.What is your favorite local museum?I like the Cafesjian Center for the Arts.What is your favorite art material to work with?For now, I really like working with natural materials like wool or soil. I really enjoy playing with tactile materials that have their own cultural and philosophical eloquence and transform their perception through scale, repetition, and other interventions. Recently I have been working on a series of soil installations that were represented in my project Body of Earth at ICA Yerevan (curated by Lilit Grigoryan). I wanted to lift the earth and give it a solid entity that you face vertically, and I wanted to stretch it however I want. It turned out to be a quite physical process of sifting, gluing, pressing, but also a very rewarding one where you work with a living material that often times directs you. As a result, I had ripped soil “sculptures” that spoke about land commodification and post-war traumas expressing human condition through land condition.

title: The Lost Pearls of New York City
description:
Art Review
                Alan Michelson's public art installation “The Oyster” on Governors Island conjures up the overlooked
body:
Art Review
                Alan Michelson's public art installation “The Oyster” on Governors Island conjures up the overlooked history of Indigenous shell middens. 
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
            Detail of Alan Michelson, "The Oyster" (2026) on Governor's Island, New York (photo Hrag Vartanian/Hyperalllergic)
    
        
            Walking down Pearl Street in lower Manhattan, you probably don’t realize that the name marks the original 17th-century East River shoreline of New York City. In fact, the street was named for a Lenape shell midden that was located on its southern section, which is also believed to have been adjacent to a Lenape canoe landing. It was one of many prominent middens that marked the region, and as Mark Kurlansky explains in his bestselling book The Big Oyster: History on the Half Shell (2006), middens are “the most common marker of a pre-European settlement anywhere in the area of the mouth of the Hudson.” These piles of oyster shells, he notes, were sometimes as much as four feet deep, sometimes buried in the ground, sometimes piled high.The early 17th-century Dutch colonists were the first to note these large piles and many of them remained well into the 19th century when the last vestiges were dismantled and then used as filler for roads and other modernization projects. Brooklyn writer Daniel Tredwell wrote in his 1839 diary that he would explore these piles with his father: “On the way out we pass many Indian shell heaps bleached as white as snow, which they much resemble at a distance. Some of them on the banks of the creek extend from fifteen to thirty feet upon the bank, and under water, in many instances entirely across the creek. These shell heaps, long ere this, has excited our curiosity and we had proposed all manner of questioning concerning their authors. These questions my father did not and could not satisfactorily answer, and we were consequently unsatisfied, and hence there was a constantly recurring inquiry.”The passage highlights that the erasure of Indigenous settlement was so thorough in 19th-century New York that it never occurred to the Tredwell family that the landmarks they visited were consciously created by those whom they displaced. Installation view of of Alan Michelson, "The Oyster" (2026), commissioned by More Art in partnership with Billion Oyster Project and Governors Island Arts (photo Timothy Schenck for Governors Island Arts)That forgetting is at the foundation of Alan Michelson’s “The Oyster” project, which opened this past weekend on Governors Island and will continue until late fall. This history, Michelson’s public artwork suggests, is still present, and equally contested, as people who live here continue to ignore the mark that the oyster has on our daily lives.
                  
                      
                        Art Review
                      
                      
                        Alan Michelson
                      
                      
                        New York

body:
Weekly Newsletter
                A never-before-published interview with Simone Forti, pleating at the Brooklyn Museum with an elite designer, and heartbreaking drawings by children held at ICE facilities. 
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
        
            Sunset over Brooklyn at the end of a workday puts my mind at relative ease. A discarded still life of white roses in a golden frame resting against a pile of black trash bags outside someone's house ends up being the most memorable art installation of the week. A new storefront church opens near my house; I see it one night when I go to buy milk for the kids. It's got a lobby with fancy-looking brown leather sofas for the faithful to sit comfortably on. I pass by a bookstore and see a photobook by Hans Wilschut titled Beirut, Epi-Centre Ville. It traces the impact of the devastating blast of 2020 on the city's streets and soul. The book piques my interest, but I keep walking and see a Honda Civic with a license plate that reads "FATIGUE." I pull my phone out to snap a picture of it, and get reminded that it's August 4, the sixth anniversary of the blast. At work, we publish a piece about desperate drawings made by immigrant children held in ICE detention camps. It breaks my heart to pieces. News about community members fighting to reinstate SAIC professor Savneet Talwar, who was unjustly put on leave for asking students to imagine treatment for a pro-Palestinian protester, put my heart back together again.Outside an open studios event in Brooklyn, I talk with an artist who makes the case for "holding on to hope.""Isn't hope for people who have no power?" I ask her. "Exactly," she says. —Hakim Bishara, editor-in-chief

	
		
			AI Companies Are Pulping Our Humanity
		
	
	
		After Spanish physician and theologian Michael Servetus was burnt at the stake in 1553 for religious heresy, only three surviving copies of his The Restoration of Christianity would be spared from the bonfire. One particular copy, now held by the University of Edinburgh library, is ironically believed to have been personally saved by the Protestant leader John Calvin, who was responsible for Servetus’s execution in Geneva. Anyone familiar with Calvin, who bragged in a letter that he had “purged the Church of so pernicious a monster,” knows that the book wasn’t preserved due to affection for Servetus, but rather a bibliophile’s sentiment — even a doctrinaire, zealous, tyrannical bibliophile. 
      
      And yet, as bizarre as Calvin’s motivations might have been, he’s still not as noxious as the artificial intelligence companies, including Anthropic, that have been involved in bulk purchasing, digitizing, and then pulping out-of-print books to train their large language models. Calvin at least had the excuse of his God; AI companies don’t even have that. | Ed Simon
